description: Hi, I am Pariton, an independent researcher from Manipur, India. I love turning open space and science data into something people can understand and use. I joined NASA's Open Science Data Repository working groups. I am a published author in IEEE Computer Society’s Feedforward magazine, a peer reviewer for IEEE conferences, and a Wikipedia editor.
summary: My project is Storm or Shine, a browser-based Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer in which a child commands a small Moon base for ten mission days. Power, Oxygen and Shielding share one small budget, while Crew Dose only goes up. Each day the player chooses three jobs, and then a real NASA storm card arrives. The player must decide whether to keep working and take the full radiation dose or shelter and take only one-third of it. This directly addresses the challenge by turning a mission decision into the game itself, instead of only showing children what astronauts do. It is important because children usually see space as results, not decisions. Storm dates come from NASA DONKI and the learning cards cite real NASA OSDR studies, so the game stays honest while teaching real space science.
details:
Storm or Shine is a single-player strategy game that runs in the browser. The idea came from a simple observation. Posters and videos show what astronauts do, but they rarely show why a crew picks shielding over power, or science over oxygen. In my game, the player has to make that choice, and I believe a choice you have to live with is remembered far longer than a fact you only read.

The player begins by choosing a mission level. Cadet is meant for ages 7 to 8 and gives more warning, while Pilot is meant for ages 9 to 12 and uses full storm strength. Every day follows four steps: Pick, Storm, Decide and Learn. First, the player chooses three jobs for the crew from five actions, which are make oxygen, grow food, add shielding, do science or rest, and each job uses Power. Then a storm card arrives with its warning time. Next, the player decides whether to keep working and take the full dose, or shelter and take one third of it. The trade-off is that sheltering protects the crew, but no other work gets done that day. Lunar night also cuts solar power on days 6 to 8, and storms come in a new order every run, so no two missions feel the same.

After every storm, a short learning card explains the science in two ways. Quick Points give children three to four short points, each with a simple symbol. The Deep Dive gives adults and curious learners precise terms, an illustration and sources. There is also a Myth vs Real section, for example the common belief that thicker metal walls always make a base safer, when in reality fast space particles can break up inside metal and add radiation, and water or plastic often protect better for the same weight.

The game uses two NASA sources. NASA DONKI provides the storm records, meaning real solar flares, coronal mass ejections and particle events, and each card shows the real date of the event. NASA OSDR, the Open Science Data Repository, provides the space biology research, and the learning cards cite real study numbers. If the live request cannot be completed, the game still works offline using clearly marked saved records, which are labelled “Archived NASA data”. I have also been open about what is simplified: storm dates are real, but strength scores, dose numbers and the ten-day mission are simplified, and the game says so on its About and data page. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.

I built it using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with AI-assisted design and coding, and I have stated this openly in my deck. The science content, the game rules, the choice of data sources and the age-based design are my own work, based on my background as a Physics graduate and an educator. I have tutored more than 80 students in Science and Mathematics from Classes 6 to 12, and that experience shaped how I wrote the cards for children. I also contribute as a member of the NASA OSDR Analysis Working Groups, which is how I became familiar with the repository.

The creative part of the project is that the lesson sits inside the dilemma. The player never has to be told that radiation is dangerous, because they feel it when their Crew Dose climbs. The intended impact is to help children understand why real mission planners make hard decisions, and to give older learners a path into the actual data and studies. As a next step, I plan to add a Mars mode where advice from Mission Control arrives with a delay, so that players learn what it means to make decisions far from home.
